---
title: "Protocol resource implementation rules"
---

Use this ruleset when adding a Posit Connect API through the Protocol resource
pattern. Public Protocols describe the supported Python interface. Shared private
classes supply the runtime behavior. Add a private adapter only when the endpoint
needs behavior that the shared implementation does not provide.

The reference implementations are
[Packages](https://github.com/posit-dev/posit-sdk-py/blob/main/src/posit/connect/packages.py)
and [Hits](https://github.com/posit-dev/posit-sdk-py/blob/main/src/posit/connect/metrics/hits.py).
The rules below describe their structure and the behavior of the shared classes.
They also identify limits that an implementation must account for.

Posit Workbench follows the same contract structure with a separate remote
procedure call (RPC) runtime.
See [Workbench Protocol resources](workbench-resources.qmd) for its implementation
and response conventions.

## Code structure

Keep the endpoint contract and any endpoint adapter in the same resource module.
Use a singular name for the item Protocol, a plural name for its collection
Protocol, and an underscore prefix for a private concrete adapter.

| Component | Responsibility | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Item Protocol | Declare dictionary access and supported item operations | `Package(Resource, Protocol)` |
| Collection Protocol | Declare sequence access and typed endpoint methods | `Packages(ResourceSequence[Package], Protocol)` |
| Shared implementation | Make requests, wrap records, and provide collection behavior | `_ResourceSequence`, `_PaginatedResourceSequence`, `_Resource` |
| Optional private adapter | Handle endpoint differences in the smallest affected method | `_Hits(_ResourceSequence, Hits)` |
| Owner property | Choose the path, identifier field, implementation, and version gate | `Client.packages`, `ContentItem.packages`, `Metrics.hits` |

The shared contracts and implementations live in
[resources.py](https://github.com/posit-dev/posit-sdk-py/blob/main/src/posit/connect/resources.py).
Pass the owner context, `self._ctx`, to child resources. Use
`self._ctx.client` for requests so the client handles authentication, URL
resolution, and HTTP errors.

## Public contract rules

1. Define items as `class Item(Resource, Protocol)`. Use `pass` when dictionary
   access is the entire item contract. Declare operations such as `destroy()`
   or `update()` only when the endpoint supports them.
2. Define collections as `class Items(ResourceSequence[Item], Protocol)`.
   Inherit the sequence contract instead of repeating its special methods.
3. Declare endpoint methods with explicit types and named parameters.
   Make filters keyword-only. Use positional-only identifiers for direct lookup,
   as in `Jobs.find(self, key: str, /)`.
4. Keep these Protocol method bodies as declarations. Use `...` rather than
   requests, filtering, serialization, or pagination logic.
5. Use `= ...` for an optional argument without a concrete default in the
   contract. Omission and `None` have different meanings. Add `| None` only when
   the interface accepts `None`.
6. Return `Iterable[Item]` from `fetch()` and `Item | None` from `find_by()`.
   An iterable supports both the list from `_ResourceSequence` and the generator
   from `_PaginatedResourceSequence`.
7. Add NumPy-style docstrings to public methods. Match the parameter types,
   return types, filtering behavior, privileges, and version requirements.
   Describe `fetch()` as returning all matching records.
8. Use `from __future__ import annotations` and import typing helpers from
   `typing_extensions`. Put imports used only for annotations under
   `if TYPE_CHECKING` when practical.

Protocols define structural types. A runtime object satisfies the public
interface through its members, without requiring an endpoint-specific item
class. The generic collection creates `_Resource` instances, not `Package` or
`Hit` instances.

Access response fields with `item["field"]`. The base `Resource.__getitem__()`
returns `Any`, so this pattern types operations without enforcing individual
response-field types.

Do not instantiate a public Protocol or require consumers to check concrete
class identity. Use `@runtime_checkable` only when runtime Protocol checks serve
a specific purpose. Those checks do not validate argument types or method
behavior.

## Minimal implementation

For an endpoint that fits the shared implementation, define only the item and
collection Protocols. This illustrative skeleton omits docstrings. Add them
before using it as an implementation.

```{.python filename="src/posit/connect/widgets.py"}
from __future__ import annotations

from typing_extensions import Iterable, Protocol

from .resources import Resource, ResourceSequence


class Widget(Resource, Protocol):
    pass


class Widgets(ResourceSequence[Widget], Protocol):
    def fetch(self, *, name: str = ...) -> Iterable[Widget]: ...

    def find_by(self, *, name: str = ...) -> Widget | None: ...
```

Wire the collection through a typed property on its owner. This example assumes
an unpaginated endpoint that returns a JSON array of records containing `guid`.
Replace the endpoint path and schema assumptions with the actual API contract.

```{.python filename="Owner property"}
@property
def widgets(self) -> Widgets:
    return _ResourceSequence(self._ctx, "v1/widgets")
```

Import `_ResourceSequence` at runtime. If `Widgets` serves only as an annotation,
import it under `if TYPE_CHECKING` in an owner module that uses deferred
annotations.

Do not add an empty `_Widgets` subclass or copy the shared methods. The
Packages module follows this minimal form. Its owner properties choose different
shared implementations for the global and content-scoped endpoints.

## Runtime selection and owner wiring

Choose the concrete implementation from the response shape.

| Endpoint response | Implementation | Requirements |
|---|---|---|
| JSON array of records | `_ResourceSequence` | Every record contains the configured identifier field |
| Page-number envelope with `current_page`, `total`, and `results` | `_PaginatedResourceSequence` | Endpoint accepts `page_number` and `page_size` |
| Different envelope or cursor pagination | Private adapter with matching pagination logic | Normalize records and preserve the public iterable contract |

`_PaginatedResourceSequence` uses
[Paginator](https://github.com/posit-dev/posit-sdk-py/blob/main/src/posit/connect/paginator.py).
It does not handle cursor pagination. The separate
[CursorPaginator](https://github.com/posit-dev/posit-sdk-py/blob/main/src/posit/connect/cursors.py)
provides cursor paging, but no shared Protocol collection wraps it directly.

Set `uid` to the response field used to construct item paths. The default is
`"guid"`. Packages uses `"name"`, Jobs uses `"key"`, and Hits uses `"id"`.
The shared implementation constructs each item path as
`<collection path>/<str(record[uid])>`.
Do not assume that this constructed path supports lookup, update, or deletion.
Declare those operations only after checking the endpoint.

For child collections, derive the path from the parent resource path when the
API uses that hierarchy. `ContentItem.packages` joins `self._path` with
`"packages"`.

Annotate the owner property with the public Protocol and return the concrete
implementation. Put `@property` above `@requires(version="...")` when the entire
endpoint has a minimum server version.

The reference wiring appears in
[client.py](https://github.com/posit-dev/posit-sdk-py/blob/main/src/posit/connect/client.py),
[content.py](https://github.com/posit-dev/posit-sdk-py/blob/main/src/posit/connect/content.py),
and [metrics.py](https://github.com/posit-dev/posit-sdk-py/blob/main/src/posit/connect/metrics/metrics.py).

- `Client.packages` returns `_PaginatedResourceSequence` with `uid="name"` and
  `page_size=1_000_000`. It requires Connect `2024.11.0`.
- `ContentItem.packages` returns `_ResourceSequence` with `uid="name"`. It also
  requires Connect `2024.11.0`.
- `Metrics.hits` returns `_Hits` with `uid="id"`. It requires Connect `2025.04.0`.

Treat these values as endpoint choices, not defaults for other APIs. The
`requires` decorator checks the version only when the context has a known
version. A property gate does not establish support for every filter. For
example, the Hits integration tests require `2026.01.0` for `content_guid`
filtering.

## Fetch and lookup semantics

`fetch(**conditions)` sends conditions as query parameters and wraps the server
response. The shared method does not perform local filtering.

`find_by(**conditions)` calls `self.fetch(**conditions)`, then returns the first
record whose dictionary contains every supplied key-value pair. It returns
`None` when no record matches. It does not guarantee a unique match or ordering.

Choose the two signatures separately. A fetch argument can describe a server
query without corresponding to an exact record field.
Hits illustrates the distinction.

| Method | Accepted conditions | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `Hits.fetch()` | `content_guid` as a string or list of strings, `start`, `end` | Server filters, including a time window and multiple content identifiers |
| `Hits.find_by()` | Scalar `id`, `content_guid`, `user_guid`, `timestamp` | Exact record-field matching after fetching |

Do not expose a list filter or time-window argument through inherited
`find_by()` unless its exact-match behavior supports that argument.
Renaming parameters inside `fetch()` does not change the original conditions
that `find_by()` compares. If an endpoint needs different lookup semantics,
override `find_by()` in its private adapter and document the behavior.

The inherited `find_by()` also forwards every condition to the server.
If the server rejects a record-field condition, adapt the fetch parameters or
separate server filtering from local matching in an override.

The separate `find(identifier)` method retrieves an item path directly. Declare
it only when the API supplies that endpoint.

The collection has no response cache. Iteration, length, indexing, slicing,
string conversion, and representation each invoke `fetch()`.
Length and indexing materialize the full result. Avoid promising cached access
or constant-time indexing. Call `fetch()` and materialize its result once when
the consumer needs repeated access.

## Private adapter rules

Add a private concrete class when an endpoint needs parameter translation,
different pagination, response normalization, or a different HTTP operation.
Keep the public Protocol stable and place wire-format details in the adapter.

For a collection adapter, put the concrete base first and the public Protocol
second, as in `_Hits(_ResourceSequence, Hits)`. Override only the affected method.
Accept `**kwargs` when delegating the declared optional filters, and return the
public item type.

This excerpt shows the fetch adaptation in Hits.

```{.python filename="src/posit/connect/metrics/hits.py"}
class _Hits(_ResourceSequence, Hits):
    def fetch(self, **kwargs) -> Iterable[Hit]:
        params = rename_params(kwargs)
        if "content_guid" in params and isinstance(params["content_guid"], list):
            params["content_guid"] = "|".join(params["content_guid"])
        return super().fetch(**params)
```

The [rename_params helper](https://github.com/posit-dev/posit-sdk-py/blob/main/src/posit/connect/metrics/rename_params.py)
translates `start` to `from` and `end` to `to`. The adapter joins a list of content
identifiers with `|`. It leaves a scalar identifier unchanged and delegates
request handling and record wrapping to the shared fetch method.

Keep omitted parameters absent. A declaration such as `start: str = ...`
does not cause the concrete `**kwargs` method to send an ellipsis.
Implement real defaults in runtime code when the interface promises them.
Do not mutate caller-owned containers while translating parameters.
In Hits, `kwargs` is a fresh dictionary, and joining the list leaves that list
unchanged.

Reuse a shared adapter helper when multiple endpoints have the same translation.
If `super().fetch()` cannot handle the response shape, use the matching paginator
or request code in the adapter and wrap records with their context and item path.
Test that behavior through the public property.

Item operations can also need an adapter. In
[repository.py](https://github.com/posit-dev/posit-sdk-py/blob/main/src/posit/connect/repository.py),
`_ContentItemRepository` overrides `_Resource.update()` to use PATCH.
The owner explicitly constructs that item adapter. A collection adapter does not
automatically replace the `_Resource` items created by the shared fetch method.

## Verification rules

Before accepting an implementation, check its public behavior through the owner
property.

- Check the HTTP method, endpoint path, query parameters, and request body where
  relevant. Use realistic response shapes and the configured identifier field.
- Cover empty results, matching records, and a `find_by()` miss. Check that
  `find_by()` selects an exact match rather than simply the first server result.
- Exercise sequence behavior and pagination across multiple pages. Check
  termination and filter forwarding when the implementation uses pagination.
- For adapters, check omitted arguments, scalar values, list values, parameter
  aliases, and unchanged caller inputs where applicable.
- Check the version gate below the supported version and at a supported version.
  Cover filter-specific version requirements when they differ.
- Run Ruff and Pyright. Generic methods use permissive types, so type checking
  alone does not prove that the endpoint fulfills the public contract.
- Add integration coverage for behavior that needs a real server, such as
  filter availability across server versions.
- Review the diff for duplicated shared behavior, unsupported public methods,
  inaccurate docstrings, and unnecessary concrete classes.

Use the
[Packages unit tests](https://github.com/posit-dev/posit-sdk-py/blob/main/tests/posit/connect/test_packages.py)
and [Hits unit tests](https://github.com/posit-dev/posit-sdk-py/blob/main/tests/posit/connect/metrics/test_hits.py)
as starting points. They use the responses package to check the public API with
HTTP fixtures. Extend coverage to match the endpoint contract.
